books.section: Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, A. Slave Rebellions
Topic 4.12 African Americans in the Early Republic, B. The Cultures of African-American Communities

primary_sources: David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, 1829

stimulus.text: "Let no man of us budge one step, and let slave-holders come to beat us from our country. America is more our country, than it is the whites—we have enriched it with our blood and tears." — David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World, September 28, 1829
stimulus.source_note: Verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker, Appeal to the Coloured Citizens of the World (Boston, September 28, 1829). Wording checked against the Documenting the American South electronic edition.

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim public-domain quotation from David Walker (1829)
stem: Southern legislatures declared Walker’s pamphlet seditious and punished anyone caught distributing it. That reaction best shows that Southern leaders

options.text: agreed with Walker’s reading of the Declaration of Independence
options.misconception: Leaders who agreed would not ban the pamphlet and punish its readers.

options.text: believed most enslaved people could not read
options.misconception: If they thought no enslaved person could read, a ban on distribution would be pointless.

options.text: thought the pamphlet would persuade Northern whites to free the slaves
options.misconception: Walker addressed Black readers, and the laws punished distribution in the South.

options.text: feared Black readers in the South would hear Walker’s call to resist

rationales.A: Banning a pamphlet is not agreement. Southern legislatures called the Appeal seditious and punished its distributors.
rationales.B: The ban itself shows the fear: the words could reach readers and move them. A book no one can read needs no ban.
rationales.C: Walker wrote to his brethren, Black Americans, not to Northern whites. The laws aimed at readers in the South.
rationales.D: Walker called on Black Americans to resist, and his pamphlet reached the South. The laws aimed to stop that call from spreading.
rationales.general:
1. Ask who the laws targeted. They punished distributing the pamphlet in the South.
2. Ask why a pamphlet needs a law. Its words could move readers to resist.
3. Name the fear. Southern leaders feared Walker’s call reaching enslaved and free Black readers.
Background: Walker, a free Black Bostonian, published the Appeal in 1829, and Southern states soon banned it.
Remember: a law banning a book tells you whose ears its words were thought to reach.
